main_topics.title: Datetime Parsing and Formatting
main_topics.summary: Parsing date text into datetime objects, formatting datetime objects back into strings, and remembering the small set of format codes that actually shows up in exams.
curation_notes: Merged the duplicate strptime-vs-strftime snippets, format-code tables, and object-vs-string reminders into a tighter core.
Kept the code patterns that let a zero-knowledge student decode exam options quickly.
Dropped noisy now()/timestamp examples from the core because they are weak for the shipped UI unless the question is explicitly about them.

must_know.title: Parse first, format last
must_know.summary: `datetime.strptime(text, format)` turns text into a datetime object; `dt.strftime(format)` turns a datetime object into text. Do math and attribute access while it is still a datetime object.
must_know.example:
from datetime import datetime
start = datetime.strptime('20-05-2024', '%d-%m-%Y')
print(start.strftime('%Y/%m/%d'))

content.text: Do arithmetic and attribute access while the value is still a datetime object.

must_know.title: Know the exam format codes by sight
must_know.summary: The recurring codes are `%Y` year, `%y` 2-digit year, `%m` month, `%d` day, `%H` hour, `%M` minute, `%S` second, and `%j` day-of-year. Constructor order is year, month, day.

pieces.title: Format codes you should recognize instantly

content.text: Constructor order is year, month, day. Formatting codes are read literally in exam answer options.

pieces.title: Parse then format with the same mental map

content.text: The recurring codes are `%Y` year, `%y` 2-digit year, `%m` month, `%d` day, `%H` hour, `%M` minute, `%S` second, and `%j` day-of-year. Constructor order is year, month, day.

must_know.title: Object vs string mental model
must_know.summary: A parsed datetime supports `.year`, `.month`, comparisons, and arithmetic. A formatted string does not. If an option formats too early, it usually breaks the later arithmetic step.
must_know.example:
dt = datetime.strptime('01-06-2023 09:30', '%d-%m-%Y %H:%M')
text = dt.strftime('%d-%m-%Y %H:%M')
# dt + timedelta(minutes=20) works
# text + timedelta(minutes=20) does not

exam_patterns.title: Decode the date format from the sample string
exam_patterns.summary: If the question shows both the input string and the format template, match separators and positions directly. This is usually enough to identify the month/day/year meaning without extra theory.

content.text: Match separators and positions directly; that is usually enough to eliminate the wrong options.

exam_patterns.title: Day-of-year questions use one of two routes
exam_patterns.summary: Either use `%j` when formatting, or compute `(dt - datetime(dt.year, 1, 1)).days + 1`. Exam distractors often forget the `+ 1` or return a timedelta instead of an integer.

exam_patterns.title: DataFrame date-column questions still reduce to parse/format rules
exam_patterns.summary: When a question builds a `Date` column from day, month, and year pieces, the winning option usually constructs a datetime in year-month-day order and then formats it with `strftime`.

useful_backup.title: `replace()` returns a new datetime
useful_backup.summary: Datetime objects are immutable. `replace(...)` gives you a modified copy; it does not change the original object in place.

useful_backup.title: `now()`, `timestamp()`, and ISO helpers
useful_backup.summary: These are fine references to have nearby, but they are backup material here because they are lower-frequency than parse/format and arithmetic traps.

useful_backup.title: Weekday, month, and year attributes are direct lookups
useful_backup.summary: Once you have a datetime object, use attributes like `.year`, `.month`, `.day`, and `.weekday()` directly instead of re-formatting the date string.

content.text: Use attributes on the datetime object itself; do not format to text first unless the question wants text output.

main_topics.title: Datetime Arithmetic and Comparisons
main_topics.summary: Timedelta arithmetic, overlap/comparison logic, and the specific traps that show up when an option turns a datetime into text too early.
curation_notes: Collapsed the arithmetic snippets into one clear 'do math before formatting' rule plus a small support layer for comparisons and overlap checks.
Kept timedelta attributes as backup rather than core because `.days` matters far more often than the full attribute list.

must_know.title: Do arithmetic before formatting
must_know.summary: Add or subtract `timedelta(...)` while the value is a datetime object. Only call `strftime(...)` after the arithmetic is finished.
must_know.example:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
start = datetime.strptime('2024-05-20', '%Y-%m-%d')
next_week = start + timedelta(days=7)
print(next_week.strftime('%Y-%m-%d'))

must_know.title: Subtracting datetimes gives a timedelta
must_know.summary: The result of `end - start` is a `timedelta`, not another datetime. The most exam-useful attribute is usually `.days`.

content.text: The most exam-useful timedelta attribute is usually `.days`.
The result of `end - start` is a `timedelta`, not another datetime. The most exam-useful attribute is usually `.days`.

must_know.title: Datetime comparisons behave like normal ordering
must_know.summary: You can compare datetimes with `<`, `>`, and `==`. Overlap questions usually combine two comparisons: one start must be before the other end, and one end must be after the other start.

exam_patterns.title: The classic trap: `strftime` too early
exam_patterns.summary: A wrong option often stores the formatted string in a list and then tries to add another week to that string in the next loop iteration.

rows: keep a datetime in the loop, then format
format early, then add a timedelta to the string
breaks because the value is no longer a datetime
content.text: This is one of the most common datetime distractor patterns.

exam_patterns.title: Overlap logic is interval logic, not equality logic
exam_patterns.summary: For event-overlap questions, the winning answer is usually the one that checks interval intersection, not exact matching times.
exam_patterns.example: Two events overlap when `a.start < b.end and a.end > b.start`.

exam_patterns.title: Constructor-vs-format confusion is a common distractor
exam_patterns.summary: Wrong options often swap constructor order, misuse `strftime` where `strptime` is needed, or try to do datetime math on a string result.

rows: build a datetime from numeric parts
content.text: Wrong options often swap these directions.

exam_patterns.title: Build recurring schedules by advancing the datetime, not the string
exam_patterns.summary: For repeated appointments or weekly schedules, keep a datetime in the loop, append the formatted text only at the edge, and advance the datetime with a timedelta each iteration.

content.text: This is the safe loop pattern for weekly date generation questions.
content.code:
current = datetime.strptime('20-05-2024', '%d-%m-%Y')
rows = []
for _ in range(3):
    rows.append(current.strftime('%d-%m-%Y'))
    current += timedelta(days=7)

useful_backup.summary: Keep this around as a fallback mental model when the format-code route is not obvious.

main_topics.title: OOP Fundamentals
main_topics.summary: What classes store, what `self` means, how constructor defaults behave, and why method-call syntax creates so many exam traps.
curation_notes: Merged the overlapping `self`, method-call, attribute, and default-argument snippets into one practical exam-facing core.
Kept the mutable-default constructor fix because it is stronger than the extra duplicate default-arg examples.
Omitted weaker near-duplicates that only rephrased the same `self` rule without adding exam value.

core_class_basics.title: Core Class Basics
core_class_basics.description: The smallest class patterns you should recognize instantly.

snippets.title: `self` means the current object
snippets.summary: Inside instance methods, read and update object state through `self.attribute`. If you assign only to a local variable, that value disappears when the method ends.

snippets.title: Method calls pass `self` automatically
snippets.summary: Use `obj.method(x)`, not `obj.method(obj, x)`. Passing the object again gives one argument too many.
snippets.example:
obj.set_date(x)      # correct
obj.set_date(obj, x) # too many args

snippets.title: Minimal class template you should recognize instantly
snippets.summary: Many OOP answer choices differ only in whether the class skeleton is written correctly. Know the smallest valid class with an initializer and one method.

content.text: Recognize the skeleton before you reason about the custom logic inside it.

constructor_defaults.title: Constructor Defaults
constructor_defaults.description: Constructor signatures, defaults, and per-object state rules.

snippets.title: Defaults in `__init__` make constructor arguments optional
snippets.summary: A parameter like `mode='land'` may be omitted by the caller, but the instance still gets that value. This matters a lot in exam distractors.

snippets.title: Use `None` for fresh per-object collections
snippets.summary: For list-like constructor arguments, use `None` as the default and create the list inside `__init__` so objects do not accidentally share state.

exam_patterns.title: Spot the extra-`self` error immediately
exam_patterns.summary: If a question shows `my_obj.method(my_obj, value)`, the error is almost always that the instance was passed manually even though Python already supplies it.

exam_patterns.title: Distinguish object state from temporary locals
exam_patterns.summary: An option that writes `name = ...` inside `__init__` or another method without `self.name = ...` usually fails to store the value on the object.

rows: stores the value on the object
content.text: If the value is meant to survive on the object, store it on `self`.

exam_patterns.title: Default-argument distractors hide in constructor signatures
exam_patterns.summary: If the class header already gives a default value, the caller is allowed to omit that argument. Wrong options often pretend the constructor call is missing something required.

content.text: If the constructor already provides a default, omitting that argument is valid.

exam_patterns.title: Trace attribute changes across method calls
exam_patterns.summary: When the exam creates one object and calls two or three methods on it, keep rewriting the object state after each call instead of trying to reason globally.

content.text: Write down the attribute after each call. Most mistakes happen when one call mutates the object and the next call reads that updated state.

useful_backup.title: Class attribute vs instance attribute
useful_backup.summary: `self.x` belongs to one object; a class attribute is shared until an instance shadows it. This is useful, but it is not as central as the `self` and method-call traps.

main_topics.title: OOP Comparison Logic
main_topics.summary: Compare-style methods where one object is only 'better' if multiple conditions are satisfied, and where the correct fallback is often `None`.
curation_notes: This topic is already thin and useful, so the draft keeps it compact instead of over-expanding it with generic comparison material.
Merged the reusable compare template and the fallback logic into one crisp rule set.

must_know.title: Check both directions explicitly
must_know.summary: In asymmetric comparison rules, `not self_better` does not mean `other_better`. Compute both conditions and only return a winner when that side truly meets the rule.
must_know.example:
self_better = self.avg > other.avg and self.reviews >= other.reviews
other_better = other.avg > self.avg and other.reviews >= self.reviews

must_know.title: Use an explicit fallback
must_know.summary: If neither object wins under the full rule, return `None` (or the stated fallback) instead of guessing that the other object must be better.

exam_patterns.title: Reject the fake `elif not avg_better` shortcut
exam_patterns.summary: A common wrong option says 'if self is not better, return the other object'. That fails whenever neither object satisfies all conditions.

rows: neither object may satisfy the full rule
you preserve the real tie / no-winner case
content.text: Do not let a missing self-win case trick you into assuming the other object must win.

exam_patterns.title: Translate the English rule into booleans first
exam_patterns.summary: Exam wording usually mixes score, review count, and a fallback. Write the rule as named boolean checks before returning anything.
exam_patterns.example:
avg_better = first.average_score() > second.average_score()
no_fewer_reviews = first.num_reviews() >= second.num_reviews()

useful_backup.summary: Keep a tiny three-case table in reserve: self wins, other wins, tie/no clear winner.

main_topics.title: Inheritance and Class Relationships
main_topics.summary: Parent-child class relationships, `super()`, and what the child keeps from the parent constructor.
curation_notes: Kept this topic lean because the current repo data is already fairly clean here.
Focused on the patterns most likely to help in shipped UI: inheritance syntax, parent initialization, and the 'child is still a parent' mental model.

must_know.title: Subclass syntax and parent initialization
must_know.summary: Write `class Child(Parent):` to inherit, and call `super().__init__(...)` when the child should keep the parent's setup logic.

must_know.title: A child object still counts as the parent type
must_know.summary: Inheritance does not replace the parent identity; it extends it. A child instance can still be treated as a parent where appropriate.

must_know.title: Inheritance quick table
must_know.summary: A compact checklist for the three cues that matter most in child-class questions.

rows: child can use inherited methods unless overridden
content.text: These three cues solve a large share of inheritance answer-choice questions.

exam_patterns.title: The child should add, not erase, the parent fields
exam_patterns.summary: Wrong options often forget to call `super().__init__(...)`, which means the inherited attributes are never initialized.

rows: the parent still initializes shared attributes
shared parent fields may never be created
set only the new child field afterward
the child adds behavior instead of replacing the parent setup
content.text: Wrong options often forget the parent initializer, which leaves inherited state incomplete.

exam_patterns.title: Use `super()` when the parent constructor still matters
exam_patterns.summary: If the parent constructor already handles shared setup, do not copy-paste it into the child unless the question explicitly asks for something else.

useful_backup.title: Three inheritance cues to remember
useful_backup.summary: Look for `class Child(Parent):`, `super().__init__(...)`, and `isinstance(child, Parent)` as the quick scan pattern.
useful_backup.example: These three cues usually identify the correct inheritance answer faster than reading every distractor in full.

useful_backup.title: Child objects inherit parent methods too
useful_backup.summary: If `Dog(Animal)` does not override a method, the child object still uses the parent version. Inheritance is not only about shared attributes.
